target: Agent 1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce scheduling barriers for many voters, especially low-income workers
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and many low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday would not reliably remove their voting-time barriers.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that a national holiday would broadly solve time-off problems for low-income voters
objection: Because the holiday would not reliably eliminate the main work-schedule barrier for low-income workers, it would disadvantage them by leaving the core obstacle in place rather than fixing it.

target: Agent 1’s preference for a national holiday over other reforms
objection: State laws requiring employers to give time off to vote, or automatic voter registration, are more reliable ways to remove voting barriers because they directly address the relevant obstacle instead of depending on private employers’ holiday practices.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a federal Election Day holiday would not change retail and service staffing enough to help workers vote
objection: Even though federal holidays do not force private employers to close, they usually influence scheduling, holiday staffing, reduced hours, or shift flexibility, so retail and service workplaces would likely make some schedule adjustments that help workers vote.

target: Agent 2’s broader assumption that retail and service employers would keep Election Day staffing essentially unchanged
objection: There is no basis for assuming retail and service employers would universally keep the same staffing patterns despite a federal holiday; holiday status commonly affects work schedules in practice.

target: Agent 2’s claim that the holiday would not meaningfully help low-income workers
objection: Because holiday-style scheduling can create reduced hours, shift swaps, or more flexibility, low-income retail and service workers would be more likely to have time to vote, so the holiday would still reduce scheduling barriers for them.

target: Agent 2’s claim that the holiday would not help low-income voters because their main problem is employer schedules
objection: The scheduling barriers at issue include school-related demands as well as work schedules, so even low-income voters can benefit from the school-day relief created by a national holiday.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday by itself would not reliably or meaningfully increase turnout
objection: A national holiday would reduce both work and school scheduling barriers and would also frame voting as a civic celebration, so it would reliably and meaningfully increase turnout rather than fail to do so.

target: Agent 2’s claim that low-income workers would still face the main time-off constraint on Election Day despite the holiday
objection: Because many eligible voters are blocked primarily by day-of scheduling conflicts, and a holiday gives time off from work and school, the holiday would remove a major barrier even if some private employers still schedule some workers.

target: Agent 2’s claim that remaining administrative or eligibility barriers prevent a holiday from meaningfully increasing turnout
objection: The existence of other barriers does not negate the impact of removing major work/school time-off barriers, so a holiday can still produce meaningful turnout gains for voters whose main obstacle is scheduling.
